title: What Does the Bible Really Say About Adultery?
paragraphs:
What Does the Bible Really Say About Adultery?
The Sin We Condemn in Others While Jesus Searches the Heart—and the Scandalous Grace That Can Still Rewrite the Story
There is a kind of silence that enters a room after adultery is discovered.
Not ordinary silence.
The kind where a phone is lying on the table.
A message has been opened.
A photograph has been seen.
A confession has finally escaped someone's mouth.
And suddenly years of memories feel contaminated.
The wedding pictures are still hanging on the wall. The children may still be asleep down the hallway. Dinner may still be sitting on the table.
But something has shattered.
Maybe you know that silence.
Maybe you caused it.
Maybe you survived it.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been doing.
Maybe there has never been another body in your bed, but there has been someone else living in your imagination.
And perhaps that last sentence made you uncomfortable.
Because when Jesus spoke about adultery, He refused to let the conversation remain safely about those people.
He brought it frighteningly close.
All the way to the heart.
The seventh commandment in Hebrew is brutally short:
לֹא תִּנְאָף — Lōʾ tinʾāph.
“You shall not commit adultery.” — Exodus 20:14.

The Hebrew verb behind the command is associated with נָאַף — nāʾaph, “to commit adultery.” In its straightforward marital sense, Scripture is prohibiting sexual unfaithfulness against the marriage covenant.
Notice what God does not say.
He does not say adultery is wrong only when somebody gets caught.
He does not say it becomes acceptable when the marriage is unhappy.
He does not say loneliness changes the command.
He does not say neglect makes betrayal righteous.
He does not say, “Unless you have fallen in love with somebody else.”
God says:
לֹא תִּנְאָף.
Do not commit adultery.
Why?
Because biblical marriage is more than a romantic arrangement maintained only while two people feel fulfilled.
It is covenant.

Genesis describes husband and wife becoming “one flesh.” Jesus Himself reaches back to that creation design when teaching about marriage. Paul later uses marriage as an astonishing picture of Christ and His church.
That means marital faithfulness is precious not because married people are perfect, but because covenant faithfulness reflects something about the character of the God who keeps covenant.
And adultery takes something God designed to say, I will be faithful to you, and replaces it with secrecy.
But then Jesus takes the command somewhere almost nobody wants Him to take it.
In Matthew 5:27–28, the Greek text records:
Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις. ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.

Jesus reminds His hearers of the command against adultery and then declares that the person who looks at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν—with the purpose of lusting after her—has already committed adultery with her ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ, “in his heart.”
Read that again slowly.
Jesus is not saying that temptation itself is identical to committing the physical act of adultery.
Nor is He saying that accidentally noticing that another person is attractive makes someone an adulterer.
The language points us toward something deliberate: the cultivated look, the entertained desire, the heart that turns another human being into an object for sexual possession.
There is a difference between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside, feeding it, giving it a room, and repeatedly returning to visit it.
Jesus goes after that room.
Because long before some affairs reach a hotel room, they have been furnished in the imagination.
Long before hands touch, boundaries can disappear in conversations.
Long before the first kiss, somebody may begin hiding messages.
Deleting history.
Changing passwords.
Waiting for a spouse to fall asleep.
Sharing emotional intimacy that rightly belongs within the marriage.
Telling themselves:
We're only friends.
Nothing physical happened.
My spouse doesn't understand me.
I deserve to feel wanted.
It's only online.
It's only fantasy.
Nobody is getting hurt.
Then Jesus walks into the carefully constructed courtroom of our excuses and says:
I am looking at the heart.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“Have I technically committed adultery?”
The deeper question becomes:
“What am I allowing my heart to become?”
That question reaches the married man scrolling secretly at midnight.
It reaches the wife whose emotional world has slowly become intertwined with someone other than her husband.
It reaches the person maintaining flirtation because the attention feels intoxicating.
It reaches pornography.
It reaches fantasy.
It reaches secret conversations.
It reaches the private comparison of your spouse with somebody who has never had to carry the ordinary weight of life with you.
And it reaches the person who has never physically crossed the line but keeps walking along its edge.
Jesus does not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what is killing us because He intends to rescue us from it.
That distinction matters.
Because some people reading this already know they are guilty.
You don't need another person screaming the word adulterer at you.
Your conscience has whispered it at 2:00 in the morning.
You remember the face of the person you betrayed.
You remember your children's confusion.
You remember promising it would never happen again.
Maybe you remember standing before God and saying vows you eventually violated.
And perhaps your deepest fear is not that people will discover what you did.
Perhaps your deepest fear is that what you did has become what you are.
So hear the Gospel carefully.
Scripture does not minimize adultery.
But Scripture also does not teach that adultery is beyond the cleansing power of Jesus Christ.

Paul gives one of the most devastating—and hopeful—passages in the New Testament when he warns the Corinthians that the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, and others living under the dominion of sin will not inherit God's kingdom.
Then come some of the most beautiful words ever spoken over ruined human histories:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Not because Corinth suddenly became populated by respectable people.
Because sinners had been washed.
Sanctified.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for never becoming scandalous.
Dead people being made alive.
Guilty people being justified.
Unclean people being washed.
Enslaved people being liberated.
Adulterers becoming faithful.
Liars becoming truthful.
Pornography addicts learning purity.
Betrayers learning covenant.
Broken husbands learning repentance.
Wounded wives learning that another person's sin does not determine their worth.
And sinners discovering that the blood of Jesus reaches places shame said could never become clean again.
This is where we must speak carefully about one of the Bible's most famous adultery narratives.
John 7:53–8:11 contains the beloved account of a woman brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.

There is an important textual fact serious Christians should know rather than hide: the earliest Greek manuscripts do not contain this passage in this location, and ancient manuscript traditions place it differently. Many modern Bibles therefore mark it with brackets or explanatory notes.
That textual history should be acknowledged honestly.
Christian faith has nothing to fear from manuscript evidence.
And the scene, as transmitted in the church's manuscript tradition, gives us an unforgettable picture consistent with truths clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
A woman is dragged into public humiliation.
The religious leaders say she was caught in adultery.
Caught.
Imagine that word from her side.
Whatever private world existed moments earlier has vanished.
Now there are eyes everywhere.
Accusations.
Religious men.
Public disgrace.
No carefully written statement.
No chance to repair her appearance.
No time to invent an excuse.
Her sin has become entertainment for a crowd.
But something is suspicious.
Adultery requires more than one participant.
Where is the man?
The Mosaic texts dealing with adultery hold both adulterous parties accountable. Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 do not create the convenient morality in which only the woman carries guilt.
Yet she stands there alone.
And they are not primarily interested in restoring her.
They are using her to trap Jesus.
Think about the cruelty of that.
A human being reduced to evidence.
Her worst moment weaponized for somebody else's religious agenda.
And Jesus refuses to play their game.
Eventually the accusers leave.
Then comes the breathtaking balance that sentimental Christianity often tears apart.
Jesus does not simply communicate:
Your sin doesn't matter.
Neither does He communicate:
Your sin is all that matters.
In the received account, He refuses to condemn her—and tells her to leave her life of sin.
Grace.
And truth.
Mercy.
And repentance.
No stone.
And no permission to return comfortably to bondage.
This is the Jesus many of us desperately need to meet again.
Because some churches have been good at the second half:
“Go and sin no more.”
But terrible at communicating mercy to the trembling person on the ground.
Others have emphasized mercy while becoming embarrassed by Christ's call to holiness.
Jesus needs neither distortion.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace looks directly at evil, understands exactly how destructive it is, and still opens a door home for the repentant sinner.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not performing enough religious suffering to convince God that you deserve another chance.
You don't.
Repentance is a Spirit-enabled turning from sin toward God.
It stops protecting the darkness.
It stops renaming adultery “finding myself.”
It stops calling lust “just being human.”
It stops calling pornography “stress relief.”
It stops calling emotional infidelity “friendship” when secrecy has already revealed otherwise.
It stops asking, “How much can I get away with?”
And begins asking:
“Jesus, what must die in me so that You can rule here?”
That may mean confession.
It may mean ending a relationship you know should never have begun.
It may mean deleting a number instead of writing one final sentimental goodbye.
It may mean radical boundaries.
It may mean handing over secrecy.
It may mean seeking mature pastoral care and wise Christian accountability.
Where appropriate and safe, it may involve truthful steps toward repairing what your sin damaged.
And forgiveness does not mean consequences magically disappear.
David's story proves that painfully.
David committed adultery with Bathsheba and then arranged circumstances leading to Uriah's death.
When Nathan confronted him, David eventually stopped hiding behind royal power.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
David was forgiven.
But consequences followed.
That is another truth modern Christianity sometimes struggles to hold together.
Forgiveness can be immediate while rebuilding trust may take years.
A betrayed spouse is not required to pretend nothing happened merely because the guilty spouse said, “God forgave me.”
Grace is not manipulation.
Forgiveness does not transform dishonesty into trustworthiness overnight.
Trust is rebuilt through truth, repentance, patience, changed behavior, accountability, and time.
If you committed adultery, you do not get to dictate how quickly the person you wounded stops hurting.
Repentance does not say:
“Why aren't you over this yet?”
Repentance says:
“I understand that what I did wounded you, and by God's grace I will stop demanding that your healing operate according to my convenience.”
And if adultery was committed against you, hear this carefully:
Another person's betrayal does not make you worthless.
Their decision to break covenant is not proof that you were insufficiently beautiful, masculine, feminine, exciting, sexual, successful, spiritual, interesting, or lovable.
You may have had real problems in your marriage.
You may have things of your own to repent of.
But marital problems do not magically turn adultery into righteousness.
Someone else's sin should not become the measuring stick of your value.
Your identity ultimately rests somewhere deeper.
In Christ.
Perhaps, though, neither category describes you.
Maybe you are the secret person.
The one nobody suspects.
You lead.
You preach.
You sing.
You post Bible verses.
Your spouse trusts you.
Your children admire you.
And there is something hidden behind a screen.
Something you keep promising yourself you can control.
Listen.
Do not wait until exposure does what repentance is inviting you to do voluntarily.
Sin grows extraordinarily expensive in darkness.
Bring it into the light.
Not onto social media.
Not before unsafe people.
But before God and, where appropriate, trustworthy mature believers who can help you walk in truth.
The goal is not public humiliation.
The goal is freedom.
Because Jesus did not die merely to improve your ability to hide.
He died and rose again to make you new.
And this is where adultery reveals something even larger than sexual sin.
Throughout Scripture, marital unfaithfulness becomes an image for spiritual unfaithfulness.
God's people repeatedly chase idols while still wanting the benefits of belonging to God.
And suddenly the adulterer is not merely that husband.
Not merely that woman.
Not merely that celebrity pastor.
Not merely that person everybody discussed online.
There is another form of infidelity.
We sing to Jesus on Sunday and give our deepest allegiance to money on Monday.
We call Him Lord while protecting the one room He is not allowed to enter.
We want His salvation without His authority.
His heaven without His holiness.
His comfort without His correction.
His forgiveness without repentance.
And if we're willing to become quiet enough, perhaps the question is not merely:
“Who committed adultery?”
Perhaps it is:
“Where have I been unfaithful to the God who has never been unfaithful to me?”
Now the stones begin falling from our hands.
Because at the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
The sexually pure person needs Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The betrayed need Jesus.
The betrayer needs Jesus.
The religious hypocrite needs Jesus.
The pornography addict needs Jesus.
The self-righteous critic needs Jesus.
You need Jesus.
I need Jesus.
And this is the scandal at the center of grace:
Jesus Christ knew the complete record before He went to the cross.
Not the edited version.
Not your church version.
Not your Facebook version.
The real one.
Every hidden thought.
Every deleted conversation.
Every betrayal.
Every night nobody knows about.
Every lie.
Every rationalization.
Every secret.
And Christ still went to Calvary.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that redemption required the cross.
At Calvary, grace is not God shrugging at adultery.
Grace is the holy Son of God bearing judgment for sinners.
The cross simultaneously tells us two things we desperately need to hear:
Your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
And—
Christ's mercy is greater than your shame can imagine.
That is why Christianity has no room for cheap grace.
But it also has no room for hopelessness.
The resurrection means your worst chapter does not possess final editorial authority over your life.
Jesus does.
Maybe your story really did become a scandal.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe only two people know.
Maybe only you and God know.
But if you will come into the light, repent, believe the Gospel, and surrender yourself to Christ, the sentence does not have to end where the scandal happened.
This is why we say:
Not because scandals are entertaining.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can rewrite the adulterer's future into faithfulness.
He can rewrite secret lust into growing purity.
He can rewrite arrogance into humility.
He can rewrite exposure into repentance.
He can rewrite shame into testimony.
He can rewrite a shattered person into someone who knows Christ more deeply than before.
That does not mean every marriage will have the same earthly outcome.
Scripture should never be used to guarantee a reconciliation timeline or outcome God has not guaranteed.
It means something even more foundational:
No repentant sinner who comes to Christ must remain spiritually defined by the sin from which Christ is redeeming them.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Sit with God for a moment.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need help, seek it.
If you have been hiding, stop making peace with darkness.
If you have been betrayed, bring your wounds to Christ instead of allowing somebody else's betrayal to become your permanent identity.

And if Jesus has already rescued you from sexual sin, adultery, pornography, betrayal, bitterness, or a life you once thought could never change, your testimony may become somebody else's evidence that grace is real.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes a small confession is the first visible crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Even send it privately to the person you cannot tag publicly.
Scripture does not permit us to make that claim. We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience, love, generosity, worship, witness, and lives surrendered to Him.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from love rather than pressure.
And beyond supporting the work, stay close because discipleship cannot survive on occasional inspiration alone.
Not because sharing earns heaven.
But because truth worth receiving is truth worth carrying.
Somewhere there may be a betrayed spouse wondering whether they still have value.
Somewhere there may be a believer standing one message away from crossing a line they cannot easily uncross.
And somewhere there may be an adulterer convinced Jesus wants nothing more to do with them.
Let this article find them.
Let Scripture confront them.
Let grace surprise them.
Let Christ call them home.
Because the most shocking thing about adultery in the Bible is not merely that God takes covenant-breaking seriously.
It is that the God who takes sin with terrifying seriousness is also the God who went to a cross to redeem sinners.
So put down the excuse.
Put down the secret.
Put down the stone.
Come into the light.
There is holiness here.
There is repentance here.
There is a cross here.
There is an empty tomb here.
And for the sinner who turns to Jesus Christ—
there is still grace here.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story, but it does not get to write the final sentence when the pen belongs to Jesus.
